The contradiction follows only if “A human being is a human being” means “A human being is a human being on the condition that he exists.” It does not. The statement is considered while the subject exists; existence is simply the setting in which it is true, not a condition that causes its truth. These are the difficulties to which the author points when he says that the argument “requires examination.” — س ره
The proof can be completed on the view of those who hold the truth, not on the Shaykh's view, since he considers existence to be conceptual. — س ره
In fact, the opposite is clear: the two supposedly necessary beings would be possible in relation to one another, not necessary in relation to one another or through another. — س ره

You may ask: how is this different from the earlier objection, which asked why the mind could not separate an existing thing into existence and something that receives it? I answer: the earlier point concerned what is logically conceivable; this one concerns what follows from their own principles. Also, here they allow particularity to belong to an essence without its being part of the essence's defining level. The earlier objection allowed it at that level. — س ره

Aristotle’s followers treat substance as a broader kind: an essence that, when it exists, is complete in itself. Suhrawardi, however, says in The Philosophy of Illumination that substancehood is not something added in the world to corporeality. Making something a body is itself making it a substance. For us, substance is the completeness of a thing's essence, which lets it stand without depending on a subject. Aristotle’s followers define it as “what exists in no subject.” “Does not exist in a subject” is a negative description, while “exists” is an added feature, as he goes on to explain. — س ره

This objection does not work. Someone who holds that the Necessary Being has an essence need not agree that all essences are either substances or accidents. The usual account distinguishes an accident, which exists in a subject, from a substance, which has an essence but exists in no subject. The Necessary Being, however, may be described without qualification as existing in no subject. Similarly, a defender of divine essence can say that God has a simple, necessary essence that requires its own existence, just as four entails evenness; substances and accidents, by contrast, have possible essences that do not require existence. Although it is false that an essence can entail existence, that is the earlier argument, so this is not a separate proof.

Still, the conclusion can be established by another argument from composition. If the Necessary Being had an essence other than existence—even a simple, specific essence—He would be a composite of essence and existence. The premise that essence is “what is set against existence” means that essence considered in itself is simply itself; it cannot, by itself, be the complete reality of God without existence. Nor can the reality of God be only an essence that causes existence, with existence remaining outside that reality. It must be the whole made up of essence and existence. This cannot be avoided by saying that one is the cause and the other its effect, just as a possible being remains composite whether existence is treated as an accident inhering in its essence, or essence as an accident inhering in existence, or their connection as real or merely analytical. What rules this out is composition itself.

For a possible being, the aspects of having existence and lacking it are distinct, just as the argument that “the simple reality is all things” assumes. Likewise, there is the aspect of an essence that does not rule out existence or nonexistence, and the aspect that rules out nonexistence. These aspects are distinct even if the mind reaches them by analysis. It judges that one occurs in the other and depends on it. That judgment of dependence is impossible in God, even at the level of analysis.

There is another proof of this central claim, which is as clear to us as the midday sun. Even the leading skeptic says in one of his books that knowing God's essence is a knot no one can undo: is existence identical with God's essence or added to it? If God had an essence, it would be possible for human beings to understand it. That is false, both rationally and by common agreement. The connection follows because an essence, wherever it exists, can in principle be understood and grasped; this is what people mean when they say that an essence is defined through itself. We are discussing the technical sense of essence: what is other than existence and, in itself, does not rule out either existence or nonexistence. Even if no one actually understands an essence, it must at least be possible to understand it, just as a common person may not actually understand the essence of a human being even though it can be understood.

If a possible being had no essence, it could not be understood either, because its external existence cannot enter the mind; otherwise it would change from external to mental existence, as explained earlier. This is why philosophers say that an individual, particular thing cannot be used to explain or understand something else. An individual thing outside the mind, distinct in itself, can be known only through direct awareness of it. Even then, the reality of existence is reached only when the mystic loses all awareness of the self. Such awareness still takes place behind a veil, or several veils—even for the First Intellect. The Necessary Being is pure existence, whose reality cannot be fully grasped.

One more proof: if God had an essence, He would not encompass every particular determination, because the specific character of any essence is incompatible with the specific characters of other essences. He must therefore be existence itself, which is compatible with every determination and extends throughout all essences. — س ره

The reason is that an unconditioned universal nature—especially when considered before it is divided into individuals—is the same as the individual in this respect. What is possible for an individual is therefore possible for its nature too. — س ره

This objection and others like it assume that existence is only a mental concept and that particular existences are merely conceptual shares in it. On that view, they must all be the same in reality. The answer assumes instead that existence is real and that particular existences are realities in their own right. — ن ره
“This feature” means being separate from essence. — ه ره

Someone might say that the same objection applies if existence is not separate from essence. In fact, the third option would be even worse: if existence together with an essence, without qualification, were the source, then every existence would be a source, since that condition is present everywhere. The reply is that the objector is not claiming that existence together with any essence at all is what makes something separate from essence. The claim is about existence together with the Necessary Being's own essence—that is, existence on the condition of that essence. — س ره

The objector is using this pattern of reasoning: God's reality is unlike every other reality; His existence, however, is like the existence of other things; therefore His reality is not identical with His existence. — س ره
The objector assumes that God is nothing but existence. The phrase “nothing other than His own reality” refers to existence, not to the Necessary Being as a separate subject. — س ره

The reply grants that God's existence shares the meaning of existence with possible things, but says the difference is that existence belongs as an added feature to possible things. The author points out that this does not answer the objection, which rests precisely on their sharing the meaning of existence.

The commentator then argues that the reply's concession is itself mistaken. God's existence entails necessity, while the existence of possible things entails possibility. Since their necessary features differ, the underlying realities must differ too; the premise that their existence is the same is therefore false. This gives another reply: on the view held by Aristotle’s followers, God's existence differs from all others in reality; on the ancient Persian view, it differs in fullness and independence. — س ره

“Existence in the absolute sense” has several meanings. First, it can mean existence with every restriction removed, even the restriction of being “absolute.” Second, it can mean all-pervading existence, also called the Breath of the All-Merciful, the Sacred Effusion, the level of the creative command “Be,” the All-Encompassing Mercy, the isthmus of all isthmuses, the second shadowed eternity, the universal Muhammadan Reality, the Truth through which things are created, or the water by which every living thing lives. Some of these names also refer to the level of divine oneness. Third, it can mean the general concept of existence that the mind abstracts from things. If either of the first two meanings is intended, there is no multiplicity. If the third is intended, everyone agrees that it is an added concept. — س ره

The difference from the previous argument is this: there, “external existence” meant the concept of existence considered as realized, and what was set against it was the essence's thinghood. Here, too, “external existence” means the concept itself, but what is set against it is the specific, real existence. — س ره

The Necessary Being is not existence taken without qualification, nor existence specifically qualified by separation from essence, nor existence left entirely unqualified. It is existence taken on the condition that nothing else is included. — ه ره
That is, it is the very reality of necessity. — ه ره
The expression is “the Necessary Being exists.” — ه ره

The sentence allows two readings. Either God's own, specific existence is itself existence and necessity; or, if “existence” means the general concept shared by things, that concept is a necessary feature of Him. The later phrase “or if He has a shared existence” refers to the first reading of “the very reality of necessity,” while “or if existence is taken in the general sense” refers to the second reading of “existence itself.” — س ره

That is, suppose someone says that God's reality is that He is existent. The question then arises whether saying He has existence repeats the same point. We can accept the wording by taking “existence” in the general sense, as a necessary feature. Or we can challenge it: He is not a thing that has existence as an added feature. In his Annotations, the Shaykh chooses this second option. — س ره

The early sages described the Necessary Being as “pure existence.” Later readers miscopied this as “His existence is necessary,” adding a letter because they thought a pronoun had dropped out of the manuscript. That reading is mistaken. — س ره
This wording occurs in The Wisdom of the Eye: the author first establishes that the concept of existence is shared, then says that it is identical with God but added to possible things. — س ره
That is, God's existence is predicated of Him without adding another feature—whether something joined to Him, a mental qualification, or a separate cause. — ه ره
Existence's being unbounded means that its light extends over all things; its spread is a mercy that reaches everything and an encompassing presence that leaves nothing outside it. — ن ره

This can mean that existence is not a universal even though it is unbounded in how it is realized: it encompasses all things, like sunlight spreading over everything it illuminates while remaining one light. In this sense, “universal” means all-encompassing; philosophers sometimes use the word this way even for a single thing, such as the single, all-encompassing heaven. Or it can mean that real existence is not a universal even though it is shared, as explained earlier: what distinguishes one existence is the very same reality that it shares with others, and what it shares is also what distinguishes it. — س ره
This points both to a clarification and to another reply: the familiar argument can be answered by denying its major premise, just as the usual answer denies its minor premise. — س ره

So God's existence cannot be present in the mind: at every level, it is identical with His own particular reality. To make it a mental existence would be to turn it into something else, which is impossible. — ن ره

Revelation says: “He sends water down from the sky, and the valleys flow according to their measure.” A poet adds: “Water flows from this turquoise sea, each vessel filled according to its capacity. No one sees from the sea more than the water in their own jar; no one knows beyond their own being.” — ه ره
Another manuscript reads: “If you were lowered by a rope into the lowest earth, you would come down upon God.”
“Witnessing through existence” means that a possible being can attend to God only through its own specific existence, as explained earlier. — ه ره

This is like becoming so absorbed in looking at your face in a mirror that you do not notice the mirror's color. The mirror and its reflection serve as instruments for seeing your face, but their color remains there in reality. A poet says: “Even if you strive, you may reach a place where your ‘you’ falls away.” — س ره
The opening line of the poem is: “You are beyond every flaw and stain; I would never claim that there are two.” — س ره

This refers to the discussion of the intellect and what it knows. In brief, some philosophers explain the “form” by which we know a thing as its essence—what makes it what it is. But essence alone cannot account for knowledge, whose nature is light and awareness. Others take it to be the essence of a material thing, with the matter mentally removed. Yet material existence belongs to matter and, because it is extended and measured, is hidden even from itself; it cannot be what knows or is directly known in itself. Once these accounts are ruled out, the accomplished philosophers mean by “form” another mode of existence, one more free of matter in eight respects, as they explain elsewhere. Since it is a mode of existence, and existence is itself a relation to God, it is what knows in every act of knowing. — س ره

In The Origin and Return, the author says that, for the most discerning philosophers in Aristotle’s school, the agent's role as a cause seems to be included in what makes it true to say that a possible thing exists. — س ره

This may be difficult for those who have not studied the deeper sciences, but it becomes clear when their principles are kept in mind. Knowledge is a great aid and guide. For example: existence, at whatever level, is good; existence is light, life, knowledge, will, and power, though these become hidden as existence descends and more visible as it rises, as in the soul and what lies above it; in what is pure and simple there are no separate features; and the unity of the Real is not numerical unity. Once such principles become settled in a seeker of truth, doubts fall away. — س ره

The Qur'an says: “Wherever you turn, there is the Face of God.” A poet puts it this way: “Whatever I look at, You have been there before me; though Your face is unseen, You are present in all things.” — ه ره

This is a subtle and profound indication: this natural witnessing and direct presence are intellectual, even though the things that reveal God and the senses through which they do so are physical. God makes Himself known to every thing; He appears to every thing and within every thing, but His appearance is free from limits and change, and His presence is not confined. The reason is that the aspect through which any thing faces its Lord and is connected to Him is itself unlimited. A limited thing cannot be without the unlimited: it depends on the unlimited and exists together with it. This does not mean that the unlimited is a part of the limited, as some ordinary people imagine. If it were truly a part, it would be limited, because a part is bounded by the other parts. The unlimited Truth is within limited things, but not as one thing enters another; and outside them, but not as one thing stands apart from another. Glory be to the One whose mercy embraces all and whose power includes all, and who is established above the Throne. — ن ره

Here is why the explanation follows from what was said. Ordinary speech is called speech because certain sounds are arranged so that, when we hear them, particular things come to mind. We might instead imagine other movements or qualities, not sounds, assigned to particular things, with the same familiar link between the sign and what it signifies. If one appeared in the mind whenever the other did, these too would truly be words, not merely words by comparison. Sounds would be no more essentially speech than those movements or qualities. That speech is sound is accidental; it is not essential to speech that it be sound. People chose separate sounds made by the mouth because they are easy to produce and quickly understood.

Every thing in the world is an existing reality with qualities that can be sensed, just as other things can. What makes something speech is not that it is sound, but that it is assigned a meaning and that the meaning repeatedly comes to mind when the sign does. Once this is understood, we can say that every existence has an inherent meaning: by a divine assignment, it points to a particular beauty or majesty in the source of all beauty and majesty. Whoever recognises that sign and its meaning recognises the thing's praise of God. Because this sign and its assignment belong to the thing itself, they remain; they exist alongside the conventional signs and meanings people give things. The first relation is vertical, leading from a thing to its divine source. The second is horizontal, linking one created thing with another. These latter, conventional links are incidental and can pass away, unlike the signs that belong to a thing's very being. God's messengers came to explain the divine signs and establish the passing away of merely conventional meanings.

I can hear acts of remembrance themselves remembering God, and acts of praise themselves praising Him. I may see someone utter God's name with a distracted mind and no attentive heart, while the very act of remembrance remembers God without the speaker noticing it. When we understand that things really are words, then, considered in relation to God, they are His speech; considered in relation to the created things and their essences, they are those things' praise and glorification. The verse points to both sides: every thing glorifies God by His own act of glorifying Himself, and also by its own act of praise. If the verse is read “but they do not understand” rather than “but you do not understand,” it means that people do not grasp this praise through reflective knowledge.

Someone may ask: suppose you have shown that existences are words. How can all beings—even bodies and physical things—be aware? We answer that this awareness has several grounds. One is that existence is awareness, will, power, and the like, especially when these become more evident at higher levels of existence. Another is the presence of the spiritual source of each kind within its members. A third is the presence of the Lord of all sources. How can the soul's presence in a body make that body aware, while the more complete presence of the Spirit of spirits could not? — س ره

The author mentions application by degrees to cover every possibility. If particular existences were wholly separate realities, there would be no room for degrees in the shared concept of existence, since degrees are possible only within one reality. — س ره

If particular existences are separate realities, then their necessary features differ. The words “as though he had not distinguished” do not mean that agreement is only in the concept and not at all in reality. That would allow one concept to be drawn from realities that differ in every respect, which would make Ibn Kammūna's objection succeed and leave no single reality of existence. It would also contradict the Razi's own words. Rather, the different levels of existence differ in one respect, which explains why their necessary features differ, and agree in another, which explains their shared meaning and underlying kinship.

Or the Razi may mean that, in general, agreement in necessary features belongs to things that agree in essence and concept. In the case of existence, however, the agreement lies in reality itself. Unlike essences, existence has no fixed nature preserved across every level, carrying the same necessary feature wherever it appears. The Razi has failed to distinguish agreement in necessary features that belongs to essences from agreement that belongs to existences. Or he may mean that sharing a concept directly establishes only that the concept is one; agreement in reality is true for other reasons, including that one concept cannot be drawn from realities that are wholly different in every respect. — س ره
It is the second kind of agreement—agreement in reality, not merely in concept—that requires agreement in necessary features. — ه ره
Degrees of existence presuppose differences within one reality. The objection assumes there can be no such difference. — ن ره

The distinction is a difference in qualities, not a separation that leaves one thing wholly apart from another. This is the fullest kind of distinction—what separates dust from the Lord of all lords. — ن ره

“No perfection still awaiting fulfillment” is not the same principle as saying that God's attributes are identical with His essence. Even the Ashʿarite, who says the attributes are added to God, also says that the Necessary Being is necessary in every respect of perfection. Some likewise say that His existence is necessary for Him and is a necessary feature of His essence. A leading example is the author of The Guidance. — س ره

This line of reasoning suits the Shaykh's position, which will be discussed later, but does not fit his claim that God's attributes are necessary—especially in the proof he takes such pains to establish. One could say that he means to exclude relational ideas merely as ideas, along with limits, deficiencies, and negations considered in themselves. — س ره

At first glance, this may suggest that the principle applies only to perfections. It does not: the Necessary Being is necessary in every respect, whether or not it concerns a perfection. If any non-perfection or relative feature were possible for Him, then a true perfection would also be possible for Him, as reflection shows. — ن ره

The proof consists of two linked conditional arguments. First: if God's reality were not enough for His attributes, one of them would come from something else. If that is so, then His reality, considered without any condition, would not make His existence necessary. Second: if God's existence is not necessary without a condition, He is not necessary in Himself. Together these show that if His reality were not enough for His attributes, He would not be necessary in Himself. That is impossible. — س ره

The objection asks how the absence of a cause can be inferred from merely not considering it. The point of the answer is that it does not follow that the cause is absent, and so the attribute's absence cannot be inferred from that. Nor does it follow that God's existence would fail to be necessary from eternity. In reality, His existence cannot be without either the attribute and its cause, or the absence of both. Otherwise, opposites would both be absent from reality. But God's existence is reality itself, with no essence behind existence and no potentiality behind actuality. If His reality were empty of both cases, it would be empty of existence altogether. That is what the proof's denial of the link is meant to prevent. — س ره

This is especially clear if an effect is nothing but its relation to its cause: turning away from the cause is then turning away from the effect itself. The author says “first” because the same reasoning could also be used against the philosophers' argument. — س ره

The argument compares existence with essences, but they differ in a crucial way. An essence can be considered at a level apart from reality, without considering other things, even if those things accompany it in reality. Existence is reality itself and has no separate level where it could be considered without regard to what exists or does not exist. — ه ره

How can things be necessary in relation to God when their own light-filled aspect is dominated by necessity and their possibility is almost hidden? Their necessity is their very relation to God, while their possibility means that they are poor and dependent. So how could God Himself be possible in relation to an effect?

The Shaykh may have meant only the abstract idea of a relation of agency, and its imagined instances. God has a true, real agency in His own reality, through which He brings forth the Sacred Effusion and the all-pervading existence; and He has a dependent, reflected agency at the level of the outpouring, in relation to what receives it. Both are necessary. The first is necessary through His own reality; the second is necessary through His reality, since it belongs to His domain and has no independent standing apart from Him. He also has a purely relational kind of agency: a mental concept that names the first two. That concept is added to His reality. The same applies to the other relational concepts people call attributes. They are no less attributes than negative descriptions are. Fatherhood, ownership, universality, and particularity are all attributes of a human being, yet their being added does not mean that something new has to happen in the external world. As with the concepts of thinghood, unity, and individuality, what is added is the concept, not an externally existing feature. This also explains why philosophers call mental concepts “attributes,” and why they sometimes speak of them as the “realities” of things.

The careful view is that mental, verbal, and written forms, considered as signs, are neither identical to the things they signify nor wholly separate from them. They are aspects in which those things appear, and are connected to them as features rather than as separate realities. Because they are ways the things appear, some judgments about the signs also apply to what they signify, and some judgments about what they signify apply to the signs. This is why religious teaching calls for respect toward the written and spoken forms of the names of God, the Prophet, and the Imams. Theologians have disagreed over whether a name is the same as what it names. The truth is that it is neither simply the same nor simply different. — س ره

This is the definition of being necessary in relation to something else. The following explanation is only an example: two things that stand in a reciprocal relation are each necessary in relation to the other, even though neither causes the other or makes the other dependent. Since this is a verbal definition, it is fine to use “necessity” in defining it; here “necessity” means that something must be so. — س ره

God's being the Creator and cause of Zayd is an illuminating relation through which He brings Zayd into being. True creation is real existence, not simply the act of saying or describing. The relation works in both directions: when existence is related to created things, it is their coming to be; when related to God, it is His bringing them into being. His bringing Zayd into being comes before Zayd, though Zayd's own existence does not.

Although Zayd's existence is possible in itself, God's bringing him into existence is necessary. Everything needed for Zayd's existence and for God's true act of bringing him into being is present in God's real causal reality, because the simple reality contains all things in a higher way. The same is true of God's reflected causal activity: just as multiplicity exists within unity, unity is present within multiplicity. God is the cause when there is no effect, and the Creator when nothing has yet been created, as the reports from the Imams say. How, then, could God's being the cause of Zayd be merely possible, as the author of the objection suggests? — س ره

The Shaykh's point is not the view his respected teacher later quotes: that changes in temporal things are changes only in relation to themselves, not in relation to God. His own point is subtler. The change of some manifestations, precisely as manifestations, does not mean that the disclosure and what is disclosed have changed. God's disclosure and the One disclosed are eternally one and unchanging. The mirrors through which that disclosure appears in some levels—the world of time and matter—do change and move. The world of the heavens and the world of souls both truly change, though in different ways; change in the first follows change in the second. We will return to the full explanation later, God willing. — ن ره

Because this claim is broader, the commentator connects it to the earlier discussion. Particularity can belong to an essence as a necessary feature, as when the kind is confined to one individual; or it can be identical with a thing, as with real existence. In either case, one may say that a thing is particular through itself. But the claim that particularity is the very reality of a thing is only the broad conclusion in the conditional argument, not its specific starting point. — س ره
This is like the different modes of existence: there are several, and each is particular through itself, since particularity is identical with existence. — س ره

The proof lists only the simplest cases. In general, two things may differ through the whole of one, through part of one, through something outside one, or through a combination in which the difference is the whole or a part of one thing but outside the other. The cases where both sides are of the same kind are easy to picture. Here are examples of mixed cases. The broader kind “animal” differs from human beings and horses through its own nature, while they differ from it through their specific features. A broader kind also differs, by itself, from its shares in particular species, while those shares differ from it through features outside the broader kind, since the species-defining features are not part of the broader kind. Or think of whiteness: it differs by itself from a black person, while the person differs from whiteness through blackness. One actual difference does not rule out another difference through the thing's own nature. Likewise, the animal nature found in a horse differs from a human being through neighing, while the human being differs from both through reason.

Since the author's aim is to list the non-overlapping cases, he gives the simplest ones and also hints at the mixed cases. In fully real, independent beings, the possible differences reduce to the three same-kind cases he names, so the options in his proof do not overlap. — س ره

In the first case, dependence in existence follows directly. In the second, it follows from the previous chapter: if even one of God's attributes were not necessary, His existence would not be necessary either. If existence came from another, it would not be identical with His particularity, since what exists through itself comes before what exists through another. — س ره
This resembles explaining away the attributes by saying that one thing stands in for another: impressive in wording, but weak in substance. — س ره

That is, the claim that an essence necessarily entails its own existence has already been disproved, both here and by the Shaykh, as reported in The Book of Discussions. And a thing's causing itself—so that it must come before itself—needs no further refutation. — س ره

“Receives existence from something else” and “depends on something else” normally mean that the other thing is external to it. This follows from what has already been shown: if an essence received existence from itself because existence necessarily followed from that essence, the result would be circular or an infinite regress. The cause must therefore be something other than the essence receiving existence. The word “other” could, however, include something joined to the essence, such as existence added to it. — س ره

The objection avoids saying that necessity comes from an outside cause, which would make the Necessary Being dependent, or from a part of the essence, which would make it composite. In substance, Ibn Kammūna chooses the first of the options in the earlier proof of unity: each reality is wholly different from the other, while the shared concept of necessity is drawn from each as a feature.

There is no contradiction between calling each Necessary Being necessary in itself and saying that necessity is predicated of it as a feature. The objection rests on the primacy of essence: “pure existence” means an essence from which existence is drawn as a feature. This will be discussed later. Some also interpret the claim that God's necessity of existence is identical with Him to mean that the effect of necessity appears from Him. That, too, assumes this view.

There is also a difference between what is called “essential” in the Posterior Analytics and what is called “essential” in the Isagoge. The commentator seems to be answering an objection: if necessity is a feature, it must belong to God after His essence, rather than at the level of His essence. But a feature need not be something added to a thing in the external world. It can be a feature only in how we think and speak about it. Here “accident” means any predicate that is not part of the subject's definition, whether or not it is an added quality. “Thing” is predicated of both the Necessary Being and possible things; “accident” is predicated of the categories of quality and quantity; and “possible” applies to possible essences. None of these predicates has to be an added thing in the world.

Someone might answer the original objection with the rule that every incidental feature must ultimately rest on something essential, and a shared incidental feature on a shared essential kind, while any essential common ground must be paired with an essential difference. That would make the Necessary Being composite. But the rule fails for “thing,” which applies to both the Necessary and the possible, and for “accident,” which applies to the highest categories, even though they share no defining essence. The rule works only for features added to subjects in the world. These are instead features abstracted by the mind. The author's replies are the sound way to answer the objection; on the view that existence is fundamental, this objection carries little force. — س ره

The author considered both senses of “feature”: something added to the subject in the world, and a predicate that applies to it without being part of its definition. Both lead to impossibility. The first sense may not be what the objector intended, but the author considers both to cover every possibility. It is also wrong to compare necessity with possibility. A possible essence may be considered at a level apart from existence, and possibility is not identical with or a part of that essence. The Necessary Being, however, cannot have a level beyond existence and necessity. So the argument establishes composition from an essential common element and an essential difference. — س ره

The author means: if we regard existence as one concept that names a single, simple, luminous reality, setting aside all particular features, we see that this pure reality includes everything of its own kind and nothing foreign to it. What is foreign to existence belongs to nonexistence and illusion. Existence is the broadest of all realities, and so cannot be two separate pure existences. The Necessary Being must be pure, intensified existence itself—not some other kind of essence from which existence and necessity are then drawn. — س ره

The argument combines a supposition of two with the claim that two are impossible. The “two” exist only in the supposition; in reality, there can be no two. The commentator distinguishes between supposing something impossible and making a supposition that is itself impossible. Sometimes we can imagine a thing from an angle that leaves open its opposite; that is an impossible thing we can suppose. But sometimes the very way we suppose it requires us to affirm what it is and deny what would contradict it. In that case the supposition itself is impossible. This is what happens here. The author makes this point in The Secrets of the Verses: whatever is pure existence, beyond which nothing is fuller, cannot even be supposed to be two, much less actually become two. — س ره
This is the proof based on the principle that simple reality contains all things. — س ره
This applies whether the two aspects are directly in God's reality or arise through further aspects that depend on His reality. — س ره

The conclusion is that a truly simple, necessary reality cannot contain “this and that”: necessity and possibility, having and lacking, light and darkness, actuality and potential, good and evil. The same applies to its attributes: knowledge and ignorance, power and helplessness, and so on. Of each pair, God has the nobler side.

Someone may object that combining existence and nonexistence, possession and deprivation, necessity and possibility—or any similar pair—is not real composition, since nonexistence is not a thing alongside existence. But the worst kind of composition is precisely a mixture of existence and nonexistence, when the nonexistence is a lack of good or perfection rather than a lack of something bad. A lack of what is bad is itself a kind of good; a lack of good is not. Nonexistence is a distinct opposite of existence. The same is true of a supposed composition of existence and essence: it amounts to existence together with nonexistence. By contrast, two aspects of existence, considered simply as existence, do not make a real composition, because what distinguishes one existence is the very thing it shares with existence as such. — س ره

The objection confuses two meanings of “necessity.” If it means intensified, real existence and the limitless intensity of light, that is not the logical feature under discussion; it is God's own reality. If it means the status of a proposition—the firmness of the relation between subject and predicate—then it is not an external thing that could cause an infinite chain. At most it is an effect of the mind when it considers something in relation to external existence. The fact that necessity applies to God means that a thinker who considers Him as real must recognise that necessity follows. — س ره

Otherwise both necessity and its opposite would be unreal, leaving no difference between them. Consider the opposite pair blindness and non-blindness. The same argument would make blindness something positive, although it plainly means a lack. The author's answer is that “unreal” here means unreal outside the mind, not unreal in every sense. — س ره

If “strengthening existence” means real, self-subsisting existence, then it is outside the logical issue at hand. If it means a stronger affirmative relation in a proposition, there is no conflict between that relation's firmness and its being a mental, non-external feature. — س ره

Contradictory concepts divide all concepts: each is either affirmed or denied. But that does not mean that every concept that is not denied has external existence. A thing may exist only in the mind, as impossible things do; and something broadly possible may also exist only in the mind. — س ره

This argument wrongly reverses the relation. A feature's existence in itself is indeed the same as its existence as a predicate of its subject. But it does not follow that everything predicated of a subject has an independent existence of its own in the world. — س ره
The argument claims two things: that these ideas exist externally, and that they are accidents in external things. Neither has been established, and reason rejects both. — س ره

A feature may have an existence of its own, like whiteness, and also have a relational existence in its subject. Or it may have no existence apart from the relational role that every predicate has as a predicate, as with blindness. In the first case, “existence” refers to the feature itself, like whiteness; in the second, it refers to the feature's being said of a subject, like blindness in a statement. In the second case, “exists” simply means “is” in a statement. — س ره

This is how the author reconciles the two schools. Aristotle's followers mean that possibility and similar concepts can truly be said of things in the world. The earlier philosophers mean that such concepts do not exist in themselves, as independent realities; they exist only through the mind's act of considering them. — س ره

This is the meaning of the philosophers' definition of a “second philosophical concept”: it applies to its subject in the mind, whether the subject is itself considered in the mind or exists outside it. When such a concept is said to exist externally, this means that the subject is related to it in an external statement; when it is said to be applied in the mind, this means that the corresponding predicate exists as a thought. — س ره

The wording is loose. The fact that there is a difference between “possibility is denied” and “the possible is denied” does not prove that possibility is a real thing. The clearer wording, used by Tusi, is: “The difference between denying possibility and denying what is possible does not prove that possibility is something real.” One can explain the intended argument by saying that, if possibility were nothing but a negation, the reasoning would erase the difference between these two phrases and then use that to prove possibility real—just as one might claim that an infinite regress proves a Necessary Being because, without one, the regress would have to exist. — س ره
This answers the first interpretation: that possibility is an independently existing thing in the world. — س ره

This answers the claim that every kind of nonexistence is defined through existence. Blindness is the absence of sight, and possibility is the absence of necessity. The same point applies to denying a denial. — س ره

The point is that if “existence” means relative affirmation, then every negation is related to some affirmation. The thing denied is not, in the simplest sense, the denial of its own denial. In that relative respect it counts as affirmative, but this does not make it an independently existing thing. — س ره
That is, when defining negation as this unrestricted kind of status. — س ره
